title: Show me I'm wrong
hook: if anyone can show me I'm wrong, I'll gladly change; truth never harmed anyone (Meditations 6.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday: gymnasium, the bump that isn't a plot. Your line was just a scratch. Did you let one accident be an accident? Day five hundred seventy-nine.

The last argument you lost. Not lost on points. Lost because the other person was right, and some part of you knew it halfway through. What happened next? Often the mind goes hunting for a technicality. A side issue. A tone to object to. Anything but the plain sentence, you're right, I was wrong. Marcus Aurelius spent his days among courtiers and petitioners, and in book six he wrote himself a note that goes the other way. It's an emperor's note, and it opens a door.
screen: `THE ARGUMENT YOU LOST.` → `HUNTING FOR A TECHNICALITY.` → `AN EMPEROR'S NOTE.`

segments.voice: First, the offer. In Meditations six, twenty-one, Marcus says that if anyone can convince him and show him that he isn't thinking or acting rightly, he'll gladly change. Not grudgingly. Gladly. Second, the reason. In George Long's translation, he says: "I seek the truth, by which no man was ever injured." Then the other half: the one who is harmed is the person who stays in their error. Being corrected feels like a loss. Marcus flips it. The correction is the gift. Staying wrong is the injury. Third, the stakes. This note was written by an emperor, and an emperor is easy to agree with. In book one he thanks his teacher Rusticus for showing him that his character needed correcting and discipline, and he praises his adoptive father, Antoninus, for listening to anyone with something useful for the common good. Read together, these lines suggest a man trying to make himself someone it was safe to correct. Fourth, the hard part. The offer has a condition: show me. He isn't promising to change his mind for anyone who's loud, or for whoever spoke last. He's asking for a reason. That's a high bar for others, and an even higher one for yourself. It means when you are shown, you really do move. Not later. Not after saving face. Changing your own mind, out loud, takes a small courage, and an ordinary day offers the chance more than once.
screen: `SHOW ME, AND I'LL GLADLY CHANGE.` · `TRUTH NEVER INJURED ANYONE.` · `SAFE TO CORRECT AN EMPEROR.` · `THE CONDITION: SHOW ME.` · then, large: `SHOW ME.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Pick one opinion you hold firmly, about a person, a plan, a habit, anything. Ask honestly: what would someone need to show me for me to change this? Picture them showing it. Notice any flinch, any urge to defend. Breathe through it. Then imagine saying, gladly, you're right. Notice how that sentence sits. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Show me I'm wrong. Marcus's standing offer to anyone with a good reason, because the truth never harmed anybody. Today's word.
Your line: show me. Today, change one mind, your own, about something small, and say so out loud. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often hold to 6.21 as a habit of inviting correction: asking colleagues or friends to point out where they're wrong, and saying plainly when they've been shown.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite way to say I'm open-minded.
what it means: being shown your error is a gift, and refusing it is the real harm.
what a scholar hears: 6.21 fits the Stoic teaching that only vice harms a person, so error held onto damages you, while losing an argument costs nothing real.
